rationale.readChoose: Match the Korean to its meaning. Counters are chosen by the kind of thing being counted.
rationale.listen: Listen for the whole word — neighbouring numbers and sound-alikes are the usual slip.
rationale.nativeSystem: Native Korean numbers count things you can point at, and they are used for hours and ages.
rationale.sinoSystem: Sino-Korean numbers are used for labels: money, dates, minutes, phone numbers, floors.
rationale.koreanToDigits: Say the parts in order. In Sino-Korean, 십 is ten and 삼십 is thirty.
rationale.countingForm: In front of a counter, 하나 둘 셋 넷 스물 become 한 두 세 네 스무. 둘 개 is not Korean; 두 개 is.
rationale.counter: A number never stands beside a noun on its own. The counter between them is chosen by what is being counted.
rationale.fill: Read the whole sentence: the words around the gap tell you which form belongs in it.
rationale.nativeBuild: Native numbers past ten are 열 plus the unit — 열하나, 열둘. The tens have their own words.
rationale.sinoBuild: Sino numbers are read left to right, part by part: 삼십오 is 삼 · 십 · 오.
rationale.irregular_month: June is 유월 and October is 시월. The regular forms 육월 and 십월 do not exist.
rationale.plain_form: Before a counter the counting form is required: 한, 두, 세, 네, 스무 — never 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷, 스물.
rationale.spacing: A counter is a separate word and takes a space: 한 개, not 한개.
rationale.system_swap: The two systems name the same value but are not interchangeable — the context decides.
rationale.sound_alike: One sound apart. Listen for the final consonant.
rationale.adjacent: Neighbouring numbers are learned as a list, so they blur. Check the value, not the position.
rationale.wrong_counter: Each counter belongs to a kind of thing — 명 for people, 마리 for animals, 개 for objects.

systems.title: Two kinds of number
systems.goal: Know both systems to ten, both zeroes, and which system a situation calls for.

pastTen.title: Past ten
pastTen.goal: Build any number in either system, and use the five forms that change before a counter.

counting.title: Counting things
counting.goal: Count people, objects and animals with the right counter, and say your age.

time.title: Time and dates
time.goal: Tell the time, say a date, and name the two irregular months.

money.title: Money and numbers you read out
money.goal: Read a price, a phone number, a floor, and the big units 만, 억, 조.

review.title: The mistakes everyone makes
review.goal: Catch the five mistakes everyone makes, then prove the system choice is automatic.

sinoBasics.title: 일 이 삼 — Sino-Korean one to ten
sinoBasics.objective: Recognise and say the Sino-Korean numbers from one to ten.
sinoBasics.step1: Korean has two sets of numbers. This set came from Chinese and is used for anything that is a label rather than a count — money, dates, minutes, phone numbers, floors.
sinoBasics.step2: One to ten: 일 이 삼 사 오 육 칠 팔 구 십. Each is one syllable, and each is also a digit you will see on prices and clocks.
sinoBasics.step3: Ten is 십. Everything past ten is built from these ten words, so knowing them well is most of the work.

nativeBasics.title: 하나 둘 셋 — native Korean one to ten
nativeBasics.objective: Recognise and say the native Korean numbers from one to ten.
nativeBasics.step1: Korea's own numbers. They are used for counting things you can point at — people, cups, animals — and for hours and ages.
nativeBasics.step2: One to ten: 하나 둘 셋 넷 다섯 여섯 일곱 여덟 아홉 열. Notice 여덟 is said 여덜: the ㅂ is silent.
nativeBasics.step3: These stop being used around ninety-nine. Above a hundred, every number is Sino-Korean whatever it counts.

zero.title: Zero is two words
zero.objective: Use 영 for zero as a quantity and 공 for the digit nought.
zero.step1: 영 is zero as an amount — in maths, in a score, in a temperature below zero (영하).
zero.step2: 공 is the digit 0, read aloud in a phone number, a room number, a code. 010 is 공일공, never 영일영.

choosing.title: Which system, and when
choosing.objective: Decide from context whether a number should be native or Sino-Korean.
choosing.step1: Native for counting things, up to about ninety-nine: 세 명 three people, 두 시 two o'clock, 스무 살 twenty years old.
choosing.step2: Sino for labels and for money and dates: 오천 원, 삼월 일 일, 삼십 분. And for every number above a hundred.
choosing.step3: One clock time uses both: the hour is native (세 시), the minutes are Sino (삼십 분). That pair is the rule in miniature.

sinoBuild.title: Sino-Korean past ten
sinoBuild.objective: Build and read Sino-Korean numbers up to a thousand.
sinoBuild.step1: Say the parts in order. 십일 is ten-one, eleven. 이십 is two-ten, twenty. 삼십오 is three-ten-five, thirty-five.
sinoBuild.step2: Watch 십육: it is written 십육 but said 심뉵. The ㄹ-sound appears between the two syllables.
sinoBuild.step3: 백 is a hundred and 천 is a thousand. There is no 일 in front of them — 백 원, not 일백 원.

nativeBuild.title: Native Korean past ten
nativeBuild.objective: Build and read native Korean numbers up to fifty.
nativeBuild.step1: 열 plus the unit gives eleven to nineteen: 열하나, 열둘, 열셋. Said as one word.
nativeBuild.step2: The tens have their own words — 스물 twenty, 서른 thirty, 마흔 forty, 쉰 fifty. They are not built from 열.
nativeBuild.step3: 열여섯 is said 열려섣: the same ㄹ-sound that appears in 심뉵.

forms.title: 한, 두, 세, 네, 스무
forms.objective: Use the five counting forms that replace 하나, 둘, 셋, 넷 and 스물 before a counter.
forms.step1: Five native numbers change shape in front of a counter. 하나 becomes 한, 둘 becomes 두, 셋 becomes 세, 넷 becomes 네, 스물 becomes 스무.
forms.step2: This is not a pronunciation slip. 둘 사람 is not accented Korean — it is wrong. It has to be 두 사람.
forms.step3: Every other native number keeps its shape: 다섯 명, 여섯 개, 열 마리. Only these five change.

counters.title: People, things and animals
counters.objective: Count people, objects and animals with 명, 사람, 개 and 마리.
counters.step1: Korean never counts a noun on its own. Between the number and the thing there is a counter word, chosen by the kind of thing.
counters.step2: 명 counts people (세 명), 개 counts objects (두 개), 마리 counts animals (고양이 두 마리). 사람 also counts people, a little less formally.
counters.step3: The noun comes first, then the number and counter: 고양이 두 마리, not 두 마리 고양이.

countersEveryday.title: Bottles, cups, tickets and books
countersEveryday.objective: Order and count everyday things with 병, 잔, 장 and 권.
countersEveryday.step1: 병 is a bottle (맥주 한 병), 잔 is a cup or glass (커피 두 잔), 장 is a flat thing such as a ticket or a sheet (표 네 장), 권 is a book (책 세 권).
countersEveryday.step2: All four take native numbers and the counting forms: 한 병, 두 잔, 세 권, 네 장.

age.title: Saying how old you are
age.objective: Give your age with 살, recognise 세, and ask an elder's age politely with 연세.
age.step1: 살 takes a native number and is what people say: 스무 살, 스물다섯 살. 몇 살이에요? asks a friend's age.
age.step2: 세 takes a Sino number and belongs on forms and in the news: 이십 세. You will read it more than say it.
age.step3: To someone older, 살 is too casual. 연세 is the honorific word for age: 연세가 어떻게 되세요?

hours.title: Telling the hour
hours.objective: Say the hour with a native number and 시, and use 반 for half past.
hours.step1: Hours take native numbers: 한 시, 두 시, 세 시, 네 시, 열 시. 몇 시예요? asks the time.
hours.step2: 반 means half: 두 시 반 is half past two. It replaces 삼십 분.
hours.step3: 몇 시예요? asks the hour. Answer with the native number and 시: 세 시예요. For the minutes you switch systems — that is the next lesson.

minutes.title: Minutes and seconds
minutes.objective: Say minutes and seconds with Sino numbers, and combine them with a native hour.
minutes.step1: Minutes and seconds take Sino numbers: 삼십 분, 십오 분, 십 초.
minutes.step2: One clock time uses both systems at once: 세 시 삼십 분 — a native hour, a Sino minute.
minutes.step3: The most common mistake is putting both in the same system. 삼 시 서른 분 is wrong twice over.

dates.title: Years, months and days
dates.objective: Say a date with 년, 월 and 일, and use the two irregular months.
dates.step1: Years, months and days are all Sino: 이천이십육 년 삼월 십오 일. Largest unit first.
dates.step2: Two months are irregular. June is 유월, not 육월; October is 시월, not 십월.
dates.step3: 일 as a day of the month is the same word as 일 for one. 삼월 일 일 is the first of March.

weekdays.title: Days of the week
weekdays.objective: Name the days of the week and ask what day it is.
weekdays.step1: The days end in 요일: 월요일 Monday, 화요일, 수요일, 목요일, 금요일 Friday, 토요일, 일요일.
weekdays.step2: 무슨 요일이에요? asks what day it is. 주말 is the weekend.

money.title: Reading a price
money.objective: Read prices in won, grouped the Korean way by ten-thousands.
money.step1: Won takes Sino numbers: 천 원, 오천 원. 얼마예요? asks the price.
money.step2: Korean groups by ten thousand, not by thousand. 만 원 is 10,000; 삼만 오천 원 is 35,000.
money.step3: A price you hear as 만 오천 원 is 15,000 — one ten-thousand and five thousands.

digits.title: Phone numbers, floors and rooms
digits.objective: Read identifiers digit by digit, with 공 for zero and 에 between groups.
digits.step1: A number that identifies rather than counts is read digit by digit: 010 is 공일공.
digits.step2: 에 goes where a dash goes: 공일공에 일이삼사에 오륙칠팔.
digits.step3: Floors, rooms and bus routes take Sino numbers: 삼 층 third floor, 오공이 호 room 502, 이백육 번 bus 206.

large.title: 만, 억, 조 — and decimals
large.objective: Read the large Korean units, percentages and decimal points.
large.step1: Korean counts in groups of four digits, not three. 만 is ten thousand, 억 is a hundred million, 조 is a trillion.
large.step2: 123,450,000 is read 1억 2345만 — the comma is in the wrong place for Korean.
large.step3: 퍼센트 is percent (오십 퍼센트), and 점 is the decimal point: 삼 점 오 is 3.5.

pitfalls.title: The five mistakes everyone makes
pitfalls.objective: Recognise and correct the five errors that mark a beginner.
pitfalls.step1: Each of these is a rule you have already met, in the place where it is easiest to forget.
pitfalls.step2: 두 살 not 둘 살. 심뉵 not 십육 as written. 유월 not 육월. A native hour with a Sino minute. A space before the counter.

mixed.title: Mixed review — which system, which form
mixed.objective: Hear or read a phrase from anywhere in the course and know which system it uses and why.
mixed.step1: Everything in this course comes down to one decision made quickly: is this a count or a label? Counts — people, things, hours, ages — take native numbers; labels — money, minutes, dates, phone numbers — take Sino-Korean.
mixed.step2: This review mixes the two. Read or listen, decide, and check the explanation whenever you hesitate. Hesitation is the thing to practise away.

gloss.phonePrefix: a phone prefix, digit by digit
gloss.phoneDash: said where a dash is written
gloss.pitfallCountingForm: Use the counting form, not the plain number
gloss.pitfallSpacing: A counter is a separate word
